raw_response:
I am 60 years old and I have been farming for 40 years. I never went to school, so I don't read those papers the county people hand out — I know farming by doing it, and I know my 5.5 mu of stevia like the back of my hand. It's just me and my husband now; our children work in the city and send a little money, but not enough for me to waste on fancy things. Stevia is our only crop because the leaves bring in cash from the buyer who drives to the village, and at my age I don't have the strength to handle wheat and corn like the younger families.

In mid-April, when the soil warms up and the frost is gone, I hire Old Zhang's rotary tiller to prepare the ground. Then I buy my stevia seedlings from the county supply store — the improved kind, about 8,000 plants per mu. I don't save my own seedlings because they get weak and the leaves turn out small. For fertilizer, I put down one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu before planting, and work it into the soil. Then in June, when the plants are knee-high, I spread half a bag of urea on top. I learned my lesson eight years ago when I tried to save money on fertilizer — the buyer paid me almost nothing because the leaves were too thin. But I don't put too much either, because fertilizer costs a lot and my husband's medicine costs even more.

I irrigate four times from my well: right after transplanting, twice when the summer heat comes, and once more before harvest in August. Pumping costs electricity money that I feel in my pocket, but if the stevia dries out the leaves get bitter and the buyer lowers the price. For spraying, I do six times total — herbicide at the beginning to stop the weeds, and insecticide every few weeks because those worms love to eat stevia leaves. I buy the cheaper bottles from the village shop.

I have to hire women from the village for about six days at transplanting and another five or six days at harvest, because bending over 5.5 mu is too much for these old bones. They cost about 100 yuan a day now, but without them the crop would rot. I expect about 520 jin per mu if the weather is kind. I'm not changing anything this year — at 60, new ideas are just risks I can't afford. I need this crop to buy my husband's medicine and put food on our table.
